items.prompt: Explain the main difference between the objectives a private sector business sets and those a public sector organisation sets.
items.canonical_answer: A private sector business is owned by private individuals or shareholders who have put their own money in, so its objectives are financial and commercial - survival, profit, growth, the value of the owners' shareholding. A public sector organisation is owned by government on behalf of the public, so its objectives are about the service delivered - reaching everyone entitled to it, meeting standards of quality and access, and staying inside the budget allocated. Both need enough revenue to cover their costs; they differ in what any surplus is for.
marking_guidance: The boundary is ownership and purpose, not size or sector of activity.
Both sides must be stated: private objectives and public objectives, not one contrasted with silence.
Credit the similarity as well as the difference - each has to cover its costs.

items.prompt: A family bakery, a municipal water depot and a sewing enterprise employing previously unemployed women all trade on the same road in Otjiwarongo. Explain why the three set different objectives.
items.canonical_answer: The bakery is owned by the family, who have their own money in it and want a return plus the freedom to keep their evenings, so its objective is profit at a level that pays for a second oven. The water depot is owned by the town council on behalf of residents, so its objective is supply hours achieved within the sum allocated to it. The sewing enterprise exists to create work for those twelve women, so its sales objective is the means of funding more training places rather than the end in itself. Identical costs and identical customers do not produce identical objectives, because the objective follows from who owns the organisation and what it exists to do.

items.prompt: Explain the mechanism by which ownership shapes the objectives an organisation sets.
items.canonical_answer: Objectives are set by whoever the organisation answers to, and different owners want different things from it. Private owners have committed their own capital and can withdraw or sell it, so they hold managers to a financial return. Government holds a public organisation to account for a service delivered to the public who fund it through taxation, so it sets service and budget measures instead. The members of a social enterprise have committed money to obtain a social result, so they hold it to that result as well as to its trading. In each case the measure applied to managers follows the interest of the owner, and managers set objectives that match the measure they are judged on.
marking_guidance: The mechanism required is: owner's interest determines the measure applied, and the measure determines the objective managers set.
An answer that only lists different objectives by sector has described the outcome without the mechanism.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between profit maximisation and profit satisficing.
items.canonical_answer: Profit maximisation means aiming for the largest profit the business can earn. Profit satisficing means aiming for a profit good enough to satisfy the owners while other things they value - free time, independence, keeping the business small enough to run alone - are also served. The distinction is not one of success and failure: a satisficing owner has chosen to stop short of the maximum in exchange for something else.
marking_guidance: The boundary is deliberate choice, not ability: satisficing is a decision to accept less profit, whereas failing to maximise is not.
Both sides must be defined.

items.prompt: A two-year-old guesthouse in Swakopmund lost a third of its bookings when the coast road closed for repairs. Explain why survival is likely to be its leading objective this year.
items.canonical_answer: The guesthouse is young, so it has little reserve cash and no long-established customer habit to fall back on, and it has just lost a third of its bookings for a reason outside its control. A business that runs out of cash has to stop trading whatever else it was aiming at, so keeping cash coming in displaces profit and growth until the road reopens. items.prompt: Namib Threads has three shareholders. It can either raise output by 40 per cent using borrowed money, or hold output steady and pay the shareholders a dividend. Explain which objective each choice serves.
items.canonical_answer: Raising output by 40 per cent serves a growth objective. Higher volume can lower average cost and strengthen the firm's position with retailers, but the stock, equipment and wages are paid for before the extra sales are collected, so the borrowing and the delay both add risk to survival. Holding output steady and paying a dividend serves the shareholders' return directly: cash reaches the three owners now rather than being tied up in the business. With only three shareholders, who may value income now over a larger business later, the second choice can be the one they prefer even though it forgoes the lower average cost.

items.prompt: Analyse how pursuing growth in market share can put a profitable business at risk.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the decision: the business sets out to win share, so it cuts price, extends credit to new customers and buys stock and equipment ahead of the demand it expects. Each of those moves cash out of the business now. The extra sales arrive later and, where credit has been extended, the money for them arrives later still. Margin per unit is lower than before because of the price cut, so a given amount of profit now needs more units. Meanwhile the commitments taken on - the equipment, the extra staff - do not fall if volume disappoints. The measurable consequence is that cash available falls even while recorded sales rise, and the effect on the business is that its survival objective is put at risk by the pursuit of its growth objective. The chain reaches that ending where the growth is funded from working capital rather than from committed long-term finance, and where the extra volume takes longer to arrive than the outgoings do.
marking_guidance: Condition: the chain holds where growth is funded from working capital and the extra sales arrive after the spending.
Mechanism: cash leaves before it returns, and lower margin per unit means more volume is needed for the same profit.
Consequence: cash available falls while recorded sales rise.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the survival of the business, and name the conflict between growth and survival.

items.prompt: Explain why a public sector organisation is usually not given a profit maximisation objective.
items.canonical_answer: The reason is ownership. It is therefore usually asked to cover its costs, or to earn a stated return, instead.

items.prompt: Explain how a council-owned bus service would decide whether to keep a route that carries few passengers.

The route may be kept at a loss where the service objective outweighs the cost per passenger, and cut where it does not.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of judging a public sector organisation on whether it stayed within its budget.
items.canonical_answer: Staying within budget measures only the cost half of value for money and says nothing about the service obtained for it, so a manager can meet the measure by cutting the service. A hospital that stays inside its allocation by leaving posts unfilled reports a good financial result and a longer waiting list, and the measure does not show the second half at all. The limitation matters because managers act on what they are held to account for, so a single cost measure leads to decisions that protect the budget at the expense of the purpose the budget was voted for. It has to be paired with measures of service quality and access before it means anything.

items.prompt: Explain the essential features that make an organisation a social enterprise rather than a charity or an ordinary company.
items.canonical_answer: Three features together. It trades: its income comes mainly from selling goods or services, not mainly from donations and grants, which is what separates it from a charity. items.prompt: Analyse how a social enterprise that raises its prices to cover its costs can end up further from its social objective.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the condition: the enterprise serves customers chosen because they have little money, and its costs exceed the price they currently pay. It raises the price to close the gap. Some of those customers cannot pay the higher price, so they stop buying. The mechanism is that the people most likely to drop out are the poorest, and they are the ones the social purpose was aimed at, so the customers who remain are on average better off than the ones who have gone. The measurable consequence is that the enterprise now covers its costs while serving fewer of its intended beneficiaries, and the share of its output reaching them has fallen. The effect on its objectives is that the financial objective has been met by moving away from the social one. The chain holds where demand from the intended group is sensitive to price; where those customers have no alternative supplier and keep buying, the enterprise gains the revenue without losing the beneficiaries.
marking_guidance: Condition: the chain starts from customers chosen for their low incomes, and depends on their demand being sensitive to price.
Mechanism: the poorest customers drop out first, because the price rise bites hardest on them.
Consequence: costs are covered while fewer intended beneficiaries are served.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the social objective of the enterprise and its beneficiaries.

items.prompt: A social enterprise supplying cheap water filters finds that it cannot cover its costs at the price its customers can afford. Evaluate whether it should give its financial objective priority over its social objective.
items.canonical_answer:
In the short run it should, and it should say plainly that this is what it is doing. The decisive criterion is that an enterprise which stops trading delivers no social result at all, so solvency is a condition of the social objective rather than a rival to it. A filter business that closes leaves its customers with no filters at any price. On the facts given, the choice is between a smaller social result and none.

The strongest argument the other way is that an enterprise which prices at full cost has become an ordinary business serving whoever can pay, and the purpose it was founded for has quietly gone while the name remains. That risk is real and is the reason the priority should be temporary and stated, not permanent and silent.

The judgement changes with what else is available. If a grant, a cross-subsidy from a higher-priced product sold to better-off customers, or a lower-cost design can close the gap, then giving the financial objective priority is unnecessary and the enterprise should pursue those first. The condition for the recommendation is therefore that no such route is open within the time the cash allows.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a clear recommendation is required, not a balanced list of the two objectives.

items.prompt: Correct this statement: "A business does not need written objectives, because everyone already knows the business wants to make money."
items.canonical_answer: The statement fails on three counts. Wanting to make money is not an objective, because it names no amount and no date, so nothing can ever settle whether it has been achieved. It supplies no criterion for choosing between options, since almost every option can be argued to make money eventually. And it does not coordinate anybody: production, sales and finance all want the business to make money and can still take decisions that cancel each other out. A written objective - raise operating profit from N$1 200 000 to N$1 500 000 in the year to June - fixes an amount, a date and a measure everyone can work to.
marking_guidance: The error is treating a general wish as an objective.
The correction must supply the three things the wish lacks: a measure, a date, and a usable criterion.

items.prompt: Explain the mechanism by which objectives coordinate the work of separate departments.
items.canonical_answer: Departments optimise their own measures, and those measures conflict: production lowers cost per unit by making long runs of one item, which leaves sales without the range customers ask for, while sales promises delivery dates production cannot meet. items.prompt: Evaluate whether setting formal written objectives is worthwhile for a sole trader running a single market stall.
items.canonical_answer:
It is worth setting one or two, and not worth building a formal system. The decisive criterion is who the objective has to coordinate. Most of the value of formal objectives lies in coordinating separate people and supplying a criterion when they disagree, and a sole trader has nobody to coordinate: she holds the whole business in her head and decides alone. What she does still gain is the measurement - a written figure for weekly takings or stock waste, with a date, tells her whether the stall is improving, which memory alone does badly.

The argument against even that is time: an hour spent on paperwork is an hour not spent selling, and a stall trades on presence. It is a real cost for a business this size, and it is why a full set of departmental objectives would be waste.

The judgement changes if she takes on staff or a second stall. At that point she is coordinating other people and cannot see everything herself, and written objectives start earning their cost. It also changes if she wants outside finance, since a provider is likely to ask what the business is aiming at and by when.

The supplier sells to mining companies that are themselves held to account publicly for conditions in their supply chains, so a problem found in its factories becomes their problem, and they may make an audit a condition of the contract. Accepting the cost therefore protects the contracts it already has and its standing when the next one is tendered. Beyond that, the audit lowers the risk of a scandal that would cost it customers, and it goes beyond the legal minimum in a way that supports the ethical position the business claims.

items.prompt: Analyse how a decision to pay suppliers a fairer price affects a business's profit in the short term and over a longer period.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the condition: the business currently buys at the lowest price available and decides to pay above it. Immediately, cost of sales rises. If the selling price is held, gross margin per unit falls and recorded profit this year falls with it - a direct, certain and measurable effect. Over a longer period the chain runs the other way, through several steps. Suppliers paid fairly are more likely to keep supplying reliably and to give this buyer priority when supply is short, which reduces lost sales. Customers who value the practice may buy more often, or accept a higher price, which restores margin. And the risk of a supply-chain scandal, with the lost contracts and management time that follow one, falls. The measurable consequence is a certain cost now against uncertain revenue and avoided cost later, so the effect on profit is negative in year one and depends thereafter on whether enough customers value the practice enough to change what they buy.

Mechanism: cost of sales rises now, while the return depends on supplier reliability and customer response later.
Consequence: profit falls in the first year; the later effect is conditional and must be stated as such.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the profit of the business and name the suppliers and customers affected.

items.prompt: A small furniture maker is two months behind on its own payments. Evaluate whether it should take on new corporate social responsibility commitments this year.
items.canonical_answer:
It should not take on new commitments this year, beyond what the law requires and what costs nothing. The decisive criterion is timing of cash: CSR spending is certain and immediate, while the return - reputation, loyalty, easier recruitment - is later and uncertain, and a business two months behind on payments cannot carry a certain cost now against an uncertain benefit later. Solvency has to come first, because a business that fails delivers nothing to anyone.

Against that, doing nothing has its own cost. Customers and staff notice conduct, and a business that treats suppliers badly while short of cash may find both harder to keep when it recovers. There are also commitments that cost little - honest description of its products, safe working practice, paying small suppliers on the agreed day once cash allows - and those should not be deferred.

The judgement changes once the payment arrears are cleared and the business has a cash buffer, and it changes sooner if a major customer makes a specific commitment a condition of trading. It would also change if the firm were publicising social claims it cannot support, since withdrawing a false claim costs nothing and protects the reputation the claim was meant to build.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required, with the exception for no-cost commitments stated.
Context: the answer must rest on this firm's arrears, not on CSR in the abstract.
Criterion: the decisive factor is the timing of certain cost against uncertain return while cash is short.
Counterargument: must acknowledge the cost of doing nothing and the low-cost commitments that remain.
Condition: must name what would change the judgement - cleared arrears, or a customer requirement.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between an aim and an objective.
items.canonical_answer: An aim is a broad long-term goal that follows from the mission - "become the region's preferred supplier of fresh produce" - which points in a direction without saying by how much or by when. The boundary is measurement and a deadline: an aim has neither, an objective has both.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between a strategy and a tactic.
items.canonical_answer: A strategy is the long-term plan of action, committing significant resources, chosen to achieve the objectives - building a cold store, entering a new country, replacing a product range. It takes a long time, costs a great deal and is hard to reverse. A tactic is a short-term, smaller-scale decision taken day to day to carry the strategy out - a two-week price promotion, re-routing a delivery, adding a Saturday shift. It is cheap, quick and easily changed. The boundary lies in time horizon, scale of resources committed and how easily the decision can be undone.
marking_guidance: The boundary is time horizon, scale of resources and reversibility.

items.prompt: Analyse what goes wrong in a business when tactics are chosen without reference to a strategy.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the condition: the business takes short-term decisions - a discount this week, a new service next week, an extra delivery run - without testing them against any long-term plan. The mechanism is that resources are finite: money and management time spent on a promotion this month are not available for the investment the strategy needed, and because no strategy was stated, nobody is counting what has been spent against it. Successive tactics also pull in different directions - a discount aimed at volume followed by a premium service aimed at margin - so customers receive an inconsistent signal about what the business is. The measurable consequences are a capital programme that slips, marketing spending that produces short bursts of volume and no lasting position, and a brand customers cannot describe. The effect on the business is that it stays busy and does not advance towards any objective.

items.prompt: Explain why the review stage matters in business decision-making.
items.canonical_answer: Review is where the objective is used a second time, as the benchmark against which the result is compared. Without it the business has an outcome but no verdict: it cannot say whether the decision worked, which of its assumptions were wrong, or whether the option it rejected would have done better. The practical cost is that the same mistake stays available to be made again, because nothing has been learned from it. Review also feeds the next decision, since the objective-setting stage of the following decision starts from what the last review found.
marking_guidance: The reason required is that review supplies the verdict and the learning, because the objective is the benchmark.
A developed answer names the cost of skipping it.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a small business should work through all six stages of decision-making before every decision it takes.
items.canonical_answer:
It should not, and the test it should apply is the size and reversibility of the decision. The decisive criterion is that the process costs management time, which in a small business is the scarcest resource there is, and that cost is worth paying only where a wrong decision would be expensive or hard to undo. Buying premises, taking on a long commitment or replacing a product range earns the full sequence. Choosing this week's promotion does not: the research would cost more than the decision is worth and the opportunity would pass while it was done.

The strongest argument the other way is that small decisions accumulate. A business that never gathers information on anything routine is guessing repeatedly, and the errors add up into a pattern nobody reviews. That case is strongest for decisions that repeat often, because there the cost of the information is spread over many uses.

The judgement changes where a decision is small but irreversible, where a repeated decision is worth researching once and applying many times, and where the owner's judgement has recently proved wrong - which is itself something only a review stage would reveal.

Context: the answer must be argued for a small business where management time is scarce.
Criterion: the decisive factor is the size and reversibility of the decision against the cost of the process.
Counterargument: must address the accumulation of small guessed decisions.
Condition: must name what would change the judgement - irreversibility, repetition, or evidence that judgement is failing.

items.prompt: Explain why a business changes its objectives as it gets older.
items.canonical_answer: An objective is set for the circumstances of a period, and the circumstances of a business change with its age. A new business has little cash, no reputation and customers who have not formed a habit, so survival is the objective that matters. Once it is established it can afford to invest and wants to, so growth and profit take over. Once it is mature and its market has stopped expanding quickly, the objective moves again - to defending market share, to raising the value of the owners' shareholding, or to spreading into new products. Leaving the earlier objective in place would direct effort at a target the business no longer needs.

items.prompt: Analyse the consequences for a business of leaving a survival objective in place after the crisis that caused it has passed.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the condition: the crisis is over - demand has returned and cash is no longer short - but the objective, and the behaviour it licensed, remain. The mechanism is that a survival objective justifies decisions that protect cash at the expense of the future: recruitment stays frozen, maintenance and marketing stay cut, and price is set to fill capacity rather than to earn margin. Each of those was correct during the crisis and is now a cost. The measurable consequences follow in order: capacity that cannot be increased when orders return, so demand goes to competitors; equipment that fails more often because maintenance was deferred; and margins held down by prices that no longer need to be low. The effect on the business is that it loses market share and profit at exactly the moment its rivals are regaining both, and the staff who accepted the restrictions as temporary begin to leave. The chain holds where managers are still judged on the cash-protecting measures the crisis introduced, since managers act on the measures applied to them.

items.prompt: A large national chain has opened a branch beside a family hardware shop that has traded profitably for twenty years. Evaluate whether the family shop should change its objectives.

The decisive criterion is that its existing objective - grow sales at the rate of the local market - now rests on an assumption that has stopped being true, because a competitor with lower buying costs and longer hours has taken part of that market. An objective that cannot be reached however well the business performs stops guiding decisions and starts demoralising the people measured against it. The sensible replacement is an objective built on what the chain cannot easily copy: advice, credit to known local builders, repairs, delivery within the hour.

The argument against changing is that objectives changed at every shock become noise, and that the family shop does not yet know how much trade it has actually lost. Twenty profitable years is evidence that the business has something the arithmetic of a price comparison does not capture.

The shop should measure the loss over one full quarter before rewriting its financial objective, while changing the strategic objective now, because building a service position takes longer than a quarter. If the measured loss turns out to be small, the financial objective can stand.

items.prompt: Oshakati Fresh Produce earned revenue of N$8 000 000 last year and has set an objective of raising revenue by 20 per cent this year. Calculate the revenue objective for the year and the monthly sales target that follows from it.
items.canonical_answer:
Formula: revenue objective = last year's revenue + (last year's revenue x percentage increase); monthly target = revenue objective / 12.

Substitution: the increase required is N$8 000 000 x 0.2 = N$1 600 000. The revenue objective is N$8 000 000 + N$1 600 000 = N$9 600 000 for the year. The monthly sales target is N$9 600 000 / 12 = N$800 000.

Interpretation: the sales department now has a figure it can be measured against every month instead of once a year, so a shortfall shows up in weeks rather than at the year end. The monthly targets also sum to the annual objective, which is what makes the cascade sound - a target of N$750 000 a month would leave the business N$600 000 short of its objective even if every month were hit.

items.prompt: Explain why an objective has to be communicated to the people expected to achieve it.
items.canonical_answer: Because behaviour only changes when somebody knows what to do differently. An objective held by the board alone is a sentence in a document: the people whose daily choices would move it are still working to whatever they worked to before. items.prompt: Oshakati Fresh Produce had revenue of N$8 000 000 last year and has set an objective of N$9 600 000 this year, cascaded as a sales target of N$800 000 a month and funded by a marketing budget of N$240 000. After three months, actual sales are N$700 000, N$760 000 and N$820 000, and marketing has spent N$85 000. Calculate the variance on sales for the quarter, explain what it tells the owners, and evaluate whether they should now raise the monthly sales target for the remaining nine months.
items.canonical_answer:
Calculation: the quarter's target is N$800 000 x 3 = N$2 400 000. Actual sales are N$700 000 + N$760 000 = N$1 460 000, and N$1 460 000 + N$820 000 = N$2 280 000. The variance is N$2 400 000 - N$2 280 000 = N$120 000 adverse, which is 5 per cent of the quarter's target. Marketing has spent N$85 000 of a N$240 000 budget, so it is running slightly ahead of an even N$60 000 a quarter.

What it tells the owners: the business is N$120 000 behind after a quarter, but the monthly figures are rising - 700, 760, 820 - and the third month is above target. The shortfall was created in the first two months and the trend has since turned, so this is a slow start rather than a failing plan, and nine months remain in which to recover N$120 000.

Judgement: they should not raise the monthly target. The decisive criterion is what the target is for - it exists to direct the sales team's effort, and a target raised because earlier months were missed punishes a team whose performance is improving. Spreading the N$120 000 over nine months requires N$120 000 / 9 = N$13 333 a month more, which turns a target the team has just met into one it misses again, with the demotivating effect that a target seen as unreachable produces. The stronger argument for raising it is that the annual objective is fixed and the arithmetic has to come from somewhere: leaving the target at N$800 000 leaves the objective N$120 000 short unless something else changes. That is a real point, and it is why the recommendation is to hold the monthly target and recover the shortfall through the marketing budget still unspent - N$240 000 - N$85 000 = N$155 000 - concentrated in the peak months. The judgement would change if the trend reversed in month four, or if the remaining marketing spending were already committed, in which case the target has to be reset and the objective itself reconsidered.

items.prompt: Kavango Poles has cut and sold treated fence poles for eleven years. Its objective for the last four has been to grow revenue by 15 per cent a year, and it has met it. This year a competitor opened a treatment plant 80 km away and undercut its prices by 12 per cent; Kavango's sales fell 20 per cent in six months and it is now one month behind on payments to its timber supplier. The owner proposes to cut prices to match. Analyse the position and evaluate what its objective should now be.
items.canonical_answer:
Position: the growth objective was set for a market Kavango had to itself and has been overtaken by an external change it did not cause. Sales down 20 per cent with payments a month late means cash, not growth, is now the binding constraint, and a growth objective held in these conditions directs effort at a target that cannot be reached and will be missed whatever the workforce does.

Analysis of the owner's proposal: matching a 12 per cent price cut restores competitiveness on price alone. The mechanism that follows is unfavourable - the competitor's plant is new and its costs may be lower, so a price war is fought on ground Kavango does not choose, and each unit now earns 12 per cent less while volume is uncertain. With payments already late, lower margin on recovered volume may worsen the cash position rather than improve it.

Working the decision through its stages: the objective should be set first - remaining solvent through the next two quarters - and only then should options be gathered and compared against it. The options are wider than matching price: selling on delivery and credit terms to builders who value them, treating poles for other producers to use spare plant capacity, agreeing revised payment terms with the timber supplier, or matching price on the products where Kavango's cost is lowest rather than across the range. Comparing those against a survival objective ranks them differently from how a growth objective would rank them.

Judgement: the objective should change from growth to survival and cash generation for the next two quarters, with a service-based competitive objective set alongside it for the year after. The strongest argument against is that abandoning the growth objective concedes the market while the competitor is still establishing itself, and eleven years of customer relationships is the asset most likely to be lost by retreating. That argument is why the survival objective should be stated as temporary and dated, with the conditions for returning to growth written down. The judgement would change if the timber supplier agreed extended terms, which would relieve the cash constraint and make a limited, targeted price response affordable.
